prompts: Add a sine wave to the height: P.y += amp * sin(P.x * freq + phase), where amp, freq and phase are float parameters on the wrangle.
Displace points vertically with a sine along X. Read the amplitude from parameter amp, the frequency from freq and the phase offset (radians) from phase.
I want ripples running along X that I can dial in with three sliders called amp, freq and phase (height, how many waves, and shifting them sideways).
code: @P.y += chf("amp") * sin(@P.x * chf("freq") + chf("phase"));

prompts: Scale the geometry uniformly about the centre of its bounding box by the float parameter scale.
Uniform scale around the bbox centre; the factor comes from a parameter named scale.
Give me a slider called scale that grows or shrinks the model in place (around its own middle, not the world origin).
code:
vector c = getbbox_center(0);
@P = c + (@P - c) * chf("scale");

prompts: Blend each point's colour toward the colour parameter tint by the float parameter mix (0 = unchanged, 1 = fully tint).
Cd = lerp(Cd, tint, mix) with tint a vector parameter and mix a float parameter.
Add a tint control: a colour picker named tint and a slider named mix that fades the existing colours into it.
code: @Cd = lerp(@Cd, chv("tint"), chf("mix"));

prompts: Put every point whose Y position is greater than the float parameter height into the point group high.
Create a point group called high containing the points above the level given by parameter height (P.y > height).
Select everything above a waterline I can slide up and down with a parameter named height; call the selection high.
code: if (@P.y > chf("height")) setpointgroup(0, "high", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: Delete every point whose point number is a multiple of the integer parameter n (n >= 1).
Remove points where ptnum % n == 0, with n read from an integer parameter called n.
Thin the points out: drop every n-th one (0, n, 2n, ...) where n is an integer slider named n.
code: if (@ptnum % chi("n") == 0) removepoint(0, @ptnum);

prompts: Create count points in a row along +X starting at the origin, spaced spacing units apart (count is an integer parameter, spacing a float parameter).
Generate a line of points on the X axis: point i at (i * spacing, 0, 0) for i = 0 .. count-1, both values read from parameters count and spacing.
Make me a row of dots going out along X from the origin; I need a count parameter for how many and a spacing parameter for the gap.
Move every point by dist units along the direction given by the vector parameter dir (normalise dir first); dist is a float parameter.
Translate the geometry: P += normalize(dir) * dist, where dir is a vector parameter and dist a float parameter.
Slide the whole thing a set distance in a direction I choose: a 3-value parameter dir for the direction and a slider dist for how far.
code: @P += normalize(chv("dir")) * chf("dist");

prompts: Colour the points in grey levels: Cd = (w, w, w) where w is the float ramp parameter profile sampled at the point's normalised height in the bounding box.
Sample a float ramp parameter named profile at relbbox(P).y and write the value to all three channels of Cd.
Shade the model from bottom to top using a ramp I can draw; the ramp parameter is called profile and should drive a grey colour.
code:
float w = chramp("profile", relbbox(0, @P).y);
@Cd = set(w, w, w);

prompts: Colour points with the colour ramp parameter grad, looked up at t = clamp(distance from the origin / maxdist, 0, 1); maxdist is a float parameter.
Cd = colour ramp grad evaluated at the point's distance to the world origin divided by parameter maxdist (clamped to 0..1).
Heat-map the points by how far they are from the centre using a colour ramp called grad; the far end of the ramp is reached at a distance set by a slider maxdist.
code:
float t = clamp(length(@P) / chf("maxdist"), 0, 1);
@Cd = vector(chramp("grad", t));

prompts: Give each point a string attribute label made of the string parameter prefix, an underscore and the point number, e.g. tree_0, tree_1.
s@label = "<prefix>_<ptnum>" where prefix is read from a string parameter named prefix.
Name the points with a label attribute: whatever text I type in a parameter called prefix, then _ and the point's number.
code: s@label = sprintf("%s_%d", chs("prefix"), @ptnum);

prompts: Add the points with positive X to a point group whose name is given by the string parameter grp.
Create a point group named by the string parameter grp and put every point with P.x > 0 in it.
Select the half of the model on the +X side and store the selection under whatever group name I type into a parameter called grp.
code: if (@P.x > 0) setpointgroup(0, chs("grp"), @ptnum, 1);

prompts: Read the float point attribute whose name is given by the string parameter attr and store twice its value in f@out.
out = 2 * (float attribute named by the string parameter attr) for every point.
I want to pick an attribute by typing its name into a parameter called attr; double that attribute's value into a new float attribute out.
code:
float val = point(0, chs("attr"), @ptnum);
f@out = 2 * val;

prompts: Flatten the geometry onto a coordinate plane: set the component of P selected by the integer parameter axis (0 = X, 1 = Y, 2 = Z) to zero.
Zero one coordinate of every point; which one is chosen by an integer parameter axis with 0, 1, 2 meaning x, y, z.
Squash the model flat along an axis I pick with a parameter called axis (0, 1 or 2 for X, Y, Z).
Jitter the points: P += (rand(ptnum + seed) - 0.5) * 2 * amt, using the vector form of rand; seed is an integer parameter, amt a float parameter.
Random offset per point in the range [-amt, amt] on each axis, computed as (vector rand(ptnum + seed) - 0.5) * 2 * amt with parameters seed (int) and amt (float).
Shake the points around a little: offset = (rand(ptnum + seed) as a vector, minus 0.5) times 2 times amt. I need a seed parameter to reroll and an amt parameter for the strength.
code:
vector r = rand(@ptnum + chi("seed"));
@P += (r - 0.5) * 2 * chf("amt");

prompts: Rotate the geometry around the world Y direction through the point given by the vector parameter pivot, by angle degrees (float parameter, positive by the right-hand rule).
Y-axis rotation about a pivot: angle (degrees) and pivot (vector) are parameters; right-hand-rule positive.
Spin the model around a vertical axis standing at a position I set with a parameter pivot, by a number of degrees from a slider angle (right-hand rule).
Store a falloff weight in f@w: 1 within distance inner of the vector parameter center, 0 beyond distance outer, with a smoothstep transition in between (inner and outer are float parameters).
w = 1 - smooth(inner, outer, distance(P, center)) using parameters center (vector), inner and outer (floats).
Make a soft spherical selection in an attribute w around a point I place with a parameter center: full strength inside radius inner, fading smoothly to nothing at radius outer.
code:
float d = distance(@P, chv("center"));
f@w = 1 - smooth(chf("inner"), chf("outer"), d);

prompts: Set pscale to a random value between the float parameters minscale and maxscale: fit(rand(ptnum), 0, 1, minscale, maxscale) with the float rand.
pscale = minscale + (maxscale - minscale) * rand(ptnum), the bounds coming from parameters minscale and maxscale.
Randomise the particle sizes between two sliders, minscale and maxscale, using rand of the point number as the random value.
code:
float r = rand(@ptnum);
f@pscale = fit(r, 0, 1, chf("minscale"), chf("maxscale"));

prompts: Delete the points on the positive side of the plane that passes through the vector parameter origin with normal given by the vector parameter normal.
Clip by a plane: remove a point when dot(P - origin, normalize(normal)) > 0; origin and normal are vector parameters.
Cut away everything in front of a plane I position with two parameters, origin (a point on it) and normal (the direction it faces).
code:
float d = dot(@P - chv("origin"), normalize(chv("normal")));
if (d > 0) removepoint(0, @ptnum);

prompts: Divide the bounding box into count equal bands along X (count is an integer parameter) and store each point's band number, 0 .. count-1, in i@stripe.
i@stripe = index of the X slab the point lies in when the bbox is cut into count equal slabs along X; the point at the maximum X belongs to the last slab.
Cut the model into a number of slices along X set by a parameter count and tag each point with its slice number in an integer attribute stripe (starting at 0).
code:
int n = chi("count");
i@stripe = min(int(floor(relbbox(0, @P).x * n)), n - 1);

prompts: Advance the particles one time step (TimeInc) under a wind/drag force: acceleration = (wind - drag * v) / mass, then v += acceleration * TimeInc and P += v * TimeInc (using the updated v). wind is a vector parameter, drag a float parameter.
One semi-implicit Euler step with force F = wind - drag * v: update v with F / mass over TimeInc, then move P with the new v. Parameters: wind (vector), drag (float).

Blow the particles with a wind I set in a parameter wind while air resistance from a parameter drag slows them; step velocity then position by one frame's time step, heavier particles (mass) reacting less.
Remap the temperature attribute from the range [inmin, inmax] to [0, 1], clamped, into f@heat; inmin and inmax are float parameters.
heat = fit(temperature, inmin, inmax, 0, 1) with parameters inmin and inmax.
Normalise temperature into a 0-1 attribute called heat using two sliders, inmin and inmax, for the cold and hot ends (values outside just clamp).
code: f@heat = fit(f@temperature, chf("inmin"), chf("inmax"), 0, 1);

prompts: Create one closed polygon with sides corners (integer parameter) on a circle of radius radius (float parameter) in the XZ plane, centred at the origin, one corner on the +X axis, corners ordered by increasing angle from +X toward +Z.
Build a regular n-gon in XZ: corner i at (radius * cos(a), 0, radius * sin(a)) with a = 2*pi*i/sides, connected in that order into a single closed polygon; sides and radius are parameters.
Make a flat regular polygon on the ground around the origin with a sides parameter and a radius parameter; start at the X axis and go around toward +Z.
Rotate the geometry about the world Y axis through the origin by speed * Time degrees, where speed is a float parameter in degrees per second (right-hand rule).
Animated Y rotation around the origin: angle in degrees = parameter speed times the current time in seconds.
Make the model turn around the vertical axis at the origin at a rate set by a slider speed, in degrees per second.
Give each primitive a string attribute shot of the form sh followed by a 4-digit zero-padded number equal to (primnum + 1) * 10, e.g. sh0010, sh0020.
s@shot on primitives = "sh" + the value (primnum + 1) * 10 padded with zeros to 4 digits.
Label every face with a shot code in an attribute called shot: sh0010 for the first, sh0020 for the next, and so on in steps of ten.
code: s@shot = sprintf("sh%04d", (@primnum + 1) * 10);

prompts: The string attribute path looks like /obj/geo1/part_05. Store its last component in s@leaf and the component before it in s@parent.
Split path at the slashes: leaf = final piece (e.g. part_05), parent = the piece just before it (e.g. geo1).
From each point's path I need two new string attributes, leaf (the name at the very end) and parent (the folder it sits in).
Each point's name ends in a number (piece0 ... piece8). Store that number as an integer attribute piece.
Extract the trailing digits of the string attribute name into i@piece.
The names look like piece7; I want just the 7 as an int attribute called piece.
code: i@piece = opdigits(s@name);

prompts: In a detail wrangle, collect the distinct values of the point string attribute name, sort them alphabetically and store them as one comma-separated string in the detail attribute all_names.
Detail attribute all_names = the sorted unique point names joined with commas (no spaces).
I need a single text on the detail, called all_names, listing every different point name once, in alphabetical order, separated by commas.
code:
string names[] = uniquevals(0, "point", "name");
s@all_names = join(sort(names), ",");

prompts: Store in s@rel the path attribute with the leading /obj/ removed, e.g. /obj/geo1/part_05 becomes geo1/part_05.
rel = path without its /obj/ prefix (only when the prefix is at the start of the string).
Chop the /obj/ off the front of every path and keep the rest in a string attribute rel.
code: s@rel = re_replace("^/obj/", "", s@path);

prompts: Write s@info as the point's name, a colon and a space, then its float attribute weight with exactly two decimals, e.g. alpha: 0.19.
info = "<name>: <weight with 2 decimal places>".
Make a readable info string per point like alpha: 0.19 (the name, then the weight rounded to two decimals).
code: s@info = sprintf("%s: %.2f", s@name, f@weight);

prompts: Set the integer attribute in_geo0 to 1 for points whose path starts with /obj/geo0/ and 0 for all others.
i@in_geo0 = 1 if path begins with the text /obj/geo0/, else 0.
Flag the points that live under /obj/geo0/ with an int attribute in_geo0 (1 yes, 0 no).
code: i@in_geo0 = startswith(s@path, "/obj/geo0/");

prompts: Store the number of characters of the name attribute in i@namelen and the number of slash-separated components of path in i@depth.
namelen = length of the string name; depth = how many pieces path has when split at /.
Two quick stats per point: namelen, how many letters its name has, and depth, how many levels its path has.
code:
i@namelen = len(s@name);
i@depth = len(split(s@path, "/"));

prompts: Store in s@flat the path attribute with every slash replaced by an underscore (so /obj/geo1/part_05 becomes _obj_geo1_part_05).
flat = path with all / characters turned into _ (the leading slash too).
Make a file-name-safe version of path called flat by swapping each / for _.
code: s@flat = re_replace("/", "_", s@path);

prompts: The path attribute contains two numbers, as in /obj/geo2/part_07. Store first * 100 + second as the integer attribute code (207 for that example).
Parse the two integers embedded in path (the geo index and the part index) and set i@code = geo * 100 + part.
Turn each path into a numeric code: the geo number times 100 plus the part number, in an int attribute called code.
code:
string m[] = re_findall("[0-9]+", s@path);
i@code = atoi(m[0]) * 100 + atoi(m[1]);

prompts: Several points share the same name. Store in i@leader the lowest point number that has the same name as the current point, and put the points that are their own leader in the point group leaders.
leader = first point (smallest ptnum) carrying this point's name; group leaders = points where leader == ptnum.

For every name pick the first point that uses it as the leader: write that point's number to an int attribute leader on all points with that name, and collect the leaders themselves in a group called leaders.
code:
i@leader = nametopoint(0, s@name);
if (i@leader == @ptnum) setpointgroup(0, "leaders", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: Each point has a unique integer id. Find the point whose id equals the current point number and store that point's position in v@partner.
partner = P of the point whose id attribute is equal to this point's ptnum.
Look up, for every point, the point that carries an id matching my point number, and copy that point's position into a vector attribute partner.
code:
int pt = idtopoint(0, @ptnum);
v@partner = point(0, "P", pt);

prompts: In a detail wrangle store the number of distinct point names in the detail attribute nnames, and an integer array detail attribute counts with, for the i-th distinct name (in the order uniqueval returns them), the number of points that have it.
Detail attributes: nnames = nuniqueval of the point attribute name; counts[i] = number of points whose name equals uniqueval(i).
Summarise the names on the detail: nnames, how many different ones there are, and counts, an int array with how many points use each (same order as the unique-value list).
Store in i@nameidx the index of the point's name within the alphabetically sorted list of distinct point names (0 for the first name alphabetically).
nameidx = position of this point's name in sort(unique point names).
Turn the names into numbers: 0 for the alphabetically first name, 1 for the next and so on, in an int attribute nameidx.
code:
string u[] = sort(uniquevals(0, "point", "name"));
i@nameidx = find(u, s@name);

prompts: In a detail wrangle, store the number of points in the point group left in the detail attribute left_count and their average position in the detail attribute left_center.
Detail attributes from point group left: left_count = number of members, left_center = mean of their P.
How many points are in the group called left, and where is their centre? Save both on the detail as left_count and left_center.
Create the point group left_near containing the points that are in group left but not in group far.
left_near = left minus far (point groups).
I have two point groups, left and far; make a third one, left_near, with the left points that are not also far.
code:
if (inpointgroup(0, "left", @ptnum) && !inpointgroup(0, "far", @ptnum))
    setpointgroup(0, "left_near", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: For every primitive in the primitive group every4, add all of that primitive's points to the point group touched.
Convert the primitive group every4 into a point group named touched (a point is in it if any of its primitives is in every4).
Take the faces in the group every4 and select their corner points into a point group called touched.
Store in f@w2 twice the point attribute weight; if the geometry has no weight attribute at all, treat weight as 1.
w2 = 2 * weight when a point attribute weight exists, otherwise w2 = 2.
Double the weight into a new attribute w2, but be safe on meshes that have no weight attribute: use 1 as the weight there.
code:
float w = haspointattrib(0, "weight") ? f@weight : 1.0;
f@w2 = 2 * w;

prompts: Multiply every point position by the float detail attribute gain.
P *= detail attribute gain (a float stored on the detail).
The geometry carries a global float called gain on its detail; scale the point positions by it.
code:
float g = detail(0, "gain");
@P *= g;

prompts: Put the points that lie on an open boundary of the polygon mesh into the point group border. (A point is on the boundary when it has more connected neighbour points than primitives using it.)
Create point group border: points whose number of edge-neighbours differs from the number of faces that reference them.
Select the rim of the surface, the points along its open edges, into a group named border.
code:
if (neighbourcount(0, @ptnum) != len(pointprims(0, @ptnum)))
    setpointgroup(0, "border", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: For every primitive store in f@avgweight the average of the float point attribute weight over the primitive's points.
avgweight (primitive attribute) = mean of weight on the points of the primitive.
Each face should get an attribute avgweight holding the average weight of its corner points.
For each primitive store the point number of its first vertex in i@first and the point number of its last vertex in i@last.
Primitive attributes first and last = point numbers of vertex 0 and of the final vertex of the primitive.
Tag every curve with where it starts and ends: int attributes first and last holding the point numbers of its first and last vertices.
code:
i@first = primpoint(0, @primnum, 0);
i@last = primpoint(0, @primnum, primvertexcount(0, @primnum) - 1);

prompts: In a vertex wrangle store in f@u the vertex's index within its primitive divided by (vertex count - 1), so the first vertex gets 0 and the last 1 (0 if the primitive has a single vertex).
Vertex attribute u = vertex index in the primitive / (number of vertices - 1).
Give every vertex along a curve a 0-to-1 parameter u by vertex order: 0 at the start, 1 at the end.
code:
int n = primvertexcount(0, @primnum);
f@u = n > 1 ? float(vertexprimindex(0, @vtxnum)) / (n - 1) : 0.0;

prompts: Put the points that are referenced by exactly one primitive into the point group corners.
Point group corners = points used by a single face.
Select the points that belong to only one polygon and name the group corners.
code: if (len(pointprims(0, @ptnum)) == 1) setpointgroup(0, "corners", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: For every closed polygon store the length of its longest edge in f@maxedge.
Primitive attribute maxedge = maximum distance between consecutive points of the polygon, including the edge from the last point back to the first.
How long is the longest side of each face? Save it per primitive as maxedge.
In a detail wrangle count the unique edges of the polygon mesh (an edge shared by two faces counts once) and store the number in the detail attribute nedges.
Detail attribute nedges = number of distinct polygon edges, counted with half-edges (count the primary half-edge of each edge).
How many edges does this mesh have? Shared edges must not be counted twice. Put the answer on the detail as nedges.
For every polygon store in i@open_edges how many of its edges are not shared with any other polygon.
Primitive attribute open_edges = number of boundary edges of the face (edges with no neighbouring face).
Count for each face how many of its sides lie on the open border of the mesh; int attribute open_edges.
For every polygon store the sorted list of the primitive numbers that share an edge with it in the integer array attribute adj, and their number in i@nadj.
Primitive attributes: adj = ascending array of edge-adjacent primitive numbers, nadj = its length.
Which faces touch each face along an edge? Save their numbers (sorted) in an int array adj and how many there are in nadj.
Put the primitives that are open (not closed) into the primitive group curves.
Primitive group curves = primitives whose closed intrinsic is 0.
The input mixes faces and open curves; select only the open curves into a group named curves.
code:
int closed = primintrinsic(0, "closed", @primnum);
if (!closed) setprimgroup(0, "curves", @primnum, 1);

prompts: In a detail wrangle store the total surface area of all primitives in the detail attribute total_area and the number of the primitive with the largest area in the detail attribute largest (the lowest primitive number if several are equally large).
Detail attributes: total_area = sum of measuredarea over all primitives; largest = primitive number with the maximum area, first one on ties.
What is the total area of the mesh and which face is the biggest? Save them on the detail as total_area and largest (take the earliest face if there is a tie).
Store in f@compact the compactness of each polygon, 4 * pi * area / perimeter^2 (1 for a circle, smaller for thin shapes).
Primitive attribute compact = 4*PI*measuredarea / measuredperimeter squared.
Rate how round or how stretched each face is with the usual 4 pi A / P squared measure, in an attribute called compact.
Store in i@shared0 the number of points each primitive has in common with primitive 0 (primitive 0 itself gets its own point count).
Primitive attribute shared0 = how many of this primitive's points are also points of primitive 0.
For each face, how many corners does it share with the very first face (face 0)? Int attribute shared0.
Average the vertex attribute uv over all vertices of each point and store the result in the point attribute uvavg.
Point attribute uvavg = mean of uv over the point's vertices.
The uvs live on vertices; I need one averaged uv per point in a vector attribute called uvavg.

In a detail wrangle count the points that lie on a UV seam, i.e. points whose vertices do not all have the same uv (difference larger than 1e-5), and store the count in the detail attribute seam_points.
Detail attribute seam_points = number of points having at least one vertex whose uv is farther than 1e-5 from the uv of the point's first vertex.
How many points sit on UV seams (their vertices disagree about uv)? Put the number on the detail as seam_points.
Delete the points that are not used by any primitive.
Remove every point that no primitive references (loose points).
There are stray points floating around that are not part of any face; get rid of them.
code: if (len(pointprims(0, @ptnum)) == 0) removepoint(0, @ptnum);

prompts: Every primitive is a two-point line segment. In a detail wrangle store the mean segment length in the detail attribute mean_len and the longest segment length in the detail attribute max_len.
Detail attributes mean_len and max_len: average and maximum of the distance between the two points of each primitive.
The geometry is a bunch of 2-point lines; I want their average length and the longest one on the detail (mean_len, max_len).
Put every point that has exactly one edge-connected neighbour into the point group ends.
Point group ends = points with neighbourcount equal to 1 (the end points of open curves).
Select the tips of the curves, the points connected to just one other point, into a group named ends.
code: if (neighbourcount(0, @ptnum) == 1) setpointgroup(0, "ends", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: Reverse the vertex order of every primitive: vertex i must reference the point that vertex (n - 1 - i) referenced before, n being the vertex count.
Flip each primitive's winding by rewiring its vertices in the opposite order (first vertex takes the last point, and so on).
Turn all the faces inside out by reversing the order of their corners.
From a primitive wrangle accumulate each primitive's area onto its points: the float point attribute area_sum must end up as the sum of the areas of all primitives touching the point.
Point attribute area_sum = total measuredarea of the faces that use the point (written from the primitives with add mode).
Spread every face's area to its corner points so that each point gets the summed area of its surrounding faces in an attribute called area_sum.
Move every point to the closest position on the surface connected to the second input.
Snap the points onto the geometry of input 1 (nearest location on its surface, not its nearest point).
Stick my scattered points onto the mesh plugged into the second input, each one to the nearest spot on it.
code: @P = minpos(1, @P);

prompts: Give each point the colour Cd of the second input's surface at the location closest to the point, interpolated across the face (not just the nearest point's colour).
Cd = input 1's Cd attribute sampled at the closest surface position (xyzdist then primuv).
Transfer colour from the mesh in the second input: every point should pick up the smoothly interpolated colour of the surface spot nearest to it.
Store the distance from each point to the closest position on the second input's surface in f@dist and the unit direction from the point to that position in v@dir.
dist = distance to the nearest surface location of input 1; dir = normalised vector pointing from the point to it.
For every point tell me how far the mesh in the second input is (attribute dist) and in which direction (unit vector attribute dir).
For every point create a new point at the position of the nearest point of the second input and connect them with a two-point polyline going from the original point to the new point.
Per point: copy the position of input 1's closest point into a new point and add an open line from the current point to it.
Draw a little line from each of my points to the nearest point of the cloud in the second input (make a new end point there).
Store in f@tavg the average of the temperature attribute over the (up to) 5 nearest points within a radius of 2 units, the point itself included.
tavg = mean temperature of the points returned by pcfind(0, P, position, radius 2, max 5 points).
Smooth the temperature a bit: each point takes the average temperature of its 5 closest points (itself included) no farther than 2 units away, into a new attribute tavg.
Treat every point as a sphere of radius pscale. Store in i@overlaps the number of OTHER points whose sphere overlaps the current point's sphere.
overlaps = count of other points with distance < pscale + their pscale (use pcfind_radius with the pscale attribute, radius scale 1).
My particles are little balls sized by pscale; count for each one how many other balls it is intersecting, as an int attribute overlaps.
code:
int nb[] = pcfind_radius(0, "P", "pscale", 1.0, @P, f@pscale, 1000);
i@overlaps = len(nb) - 1;

prompts: Cast a ray from each point along its normal N, at most 3 units long, against the second input. Store 1 in i@hit if it hits and 0 if not, and the distance to the hit in f@hitdist (-1 when there is no hit).
intersect input 1 with a ray from P in direction normalize(N) * 3: hit = whether a primitive was hit, hitdist = distance from P to the hit position or -1.

Shoot a ray out of every point in the direction of its normal, up to 3 units, and tell me if it reaches the mesh in the second input (attribute hit) and how far away that is (attribute hitdist, -1 if nothing).
Translate the geometry so that the centre of the bottom face of its bounding box sits at the world origin.
Move the object so its bbox is centred in X and Z and its lowest Y is at 0.
Put the model on the floor at the origin: centred left-right and front-back, with its lowest point touching y = 0.
Centre the geometry at the origin and scale it uniformly so the largest dimension of its bounding box becomes exactly 1.
P = (P - bbox centre) / max(bbox size x, y, z).
Normalise the model's size: centred on the origin and scaled evenly so its longest side measures one unit.
For each point compute the distance d1 to its nearest other point and d2 to its second nearest other point, and store d1 / d2 in f@ratio.
ratio = (distance to the closest other point) / (distance to the second closest other point).
How isolated is each point's nearest neighbour compared with the next one? Store nearest distance divided by second-nearest distance in an attribute ratio.

Store a vortex force around the world Y axis in v@force: direction cross((0,1,0), r) where r = (P.x, 0, P.z) is the horizontal offset from the axis, magnitude scaled by the float parameter strength and divided by max(|r|^2, 0.01).

Make a whirlpool force that spins the particles around the vertical axis, stronger near the axis, with a slider called strength; write it to the force attribute.

Pull the particles toward a point I set with a parameter target like gravity does: stronger when close (one over distance squared), scaled by a parameter gm and by each particle's mass. Write the force attribute.

Semi-implicit Euler step of a spring-damper toward rest: acc = k * (rest - P) - damp * v; v += acc * TimeInc; P += v * TimeInc.
Make the points spring back toward where they belong (their rest attribute) with a stiffness slider k and a damping slider damp; do one simulation step of velocity then position.

Constraints that are stretched too far should snap: anything longer than its rest length by more than a percentage set in a parameter limit gets deleted, points stay.

Compute the pull of all the springs on each point: every stretched spring drags its two ends toward each other in proportion to its stiffness and its stretch. Sum these into a point attribute called force.
Multiply the restlength attribute of every constraint primitive by the float parameter restscale.

Shrink or grow the cloth by scaling all rest lengths (the restlength attribute) with a slider called restscale.

Animate a bounce: add abs(sin(Time * pi)) * height to P.y, where height is a float parameter, so the object touches down once per second.
P.y += height * |sin(pi * Time)| with height read from a parameter.
Make the object hop up and down, one hop per second, as high as a slider called height says.

h = pcopen(0, "P", P, radius, 8); i@found = pcnumfound(h); f@max_ps = max over pciterate(h) of the pscale read with pcimport; pcclose(h).
Look at up to eight points within a search radius (parameter radius) around each point, itself included: how many are there (found) and what is the biggest pscale among them (max_ps)?
In a volume wrangle on an SDF named surface, shrink the shape inward by exactly one voxel diagonal: add volumevoxeldiameter of the volume (primitive 0) to every voxel value.
f@surface += volumevoxeldiameter(0, 0).
Erode the signed distance field surface by the length of one voxel's diagonal, so the zero surface moves inward by that much whatever the resolution is.
code: f@surface += volumevoxeldiameter(0, 0);

prompts: In a volume wrangle replace each voxel of the volume density by the average of itself and its two neighbours along Y (the voxels at index iy - 1 and iy + 1, read from the input with volumeindex on primitive 0).
f@density = (volumeindex(0, 0, set(ix, iy - 1, iz)) + density + volumeindex(0, 0, set(ix, iy + 1, iz))) / 3.
Blur the density volume a little in the vertical direction only: every voxel becomes the mean of the voxel below, itself and the voxel above.
Each point has a float attribute freq (55 or higher). Store in i@octave how many whole octaves it lies above 55: the floor of the base-2 logarithm of freq / 55.
i@octave = floor(log(freq / 55) / log(2)).
Sort the frequencies in freq into octaves counted from 55 Hz: 55 up to 110 is octave 0, 110 up to 220 is octave 1, and so on (integer attribute octave).
code: i@octave = int(floor(log(f@freq / 55) / log(2)));

prompts: Split the X coordinate of each point into f@whole, its whole part rounded toward zero (so -3.3 gives -3), and f@rest, the remainder P.x - whole.
f@whole = trunc(P.x); f@rest = P.x - whole.
Separate each point's x position into the part before the decimal point (whole, keeping the sign: -2.57 becomes -2) and the part after it (rest: -0.57).
code:
f@whole = trunc(@P.x);
f@rest = @P.x - f@whole;

prompts: Each point has a float attribute vol, the volume of a sphere. Set pscale to the radius of that sphere: the cube root of 3 * vol / (4 * PI).
f@pscale = cbrt(3 * vol / (4 * PI)).
The attribute vol says how much volume each particle's sphere should have; set pscale to the matching sphere radius.
code: f@pscale = cbrt(3 * f@vol / (4 * PI));

prompts: With the vector parameters a and b, store in f@dseg the distance from each point to the line segment from a to b, and in f@dline its distance to the infinite line through a and b.
f@dseg = distance_pointsegment(P, a, b); f@dline = distance_pointline(P, a, b).
Two parameters a and b mark the ends of a bar. I need each point's distance to the bar itself (dseg) and to the endless straight line the bar lies on (dline).

With the vector parameter eye as the viewer position, store in v@refl the mirror reflection of the viewing direction at each point: reflect the normalised direction from eye to the point about the normalised normal N.
v@refl = reflect(normalize(P - chv("eye")), normalize(N)).
Imagine looking at the surface from a point eye (a vector parameter): in which direction does the line of sight bounce off at each point? Store that direction as refl.
code:
vector i = normalize(@P - chv("eye"));
v@refl = reflect(i, normalize(v@N));

prompts: Treat the float array attribute samples as evenly spaced keys of a piecewise linear curve over 0..1 and evaluate it at the point's weight attribute: f@s = spline("linear", weight, samples).
f@s = spline("linear", f@weight, f[]@samples).
Use each point's samples list like a little ramp: first entry at 0, last at 1, straight lines in between. Look it up at the position given by weight and store the result in s.
code: f@s = spline("linear", f@weight, f[]@samples);

prompts: Store in i@dsum the sum of the decimal digits of the integer attribute id (for example id 163 gives 10).
n = id; dsum = 0; while (n > 0) { dsum += n % 10; n /= 10; }
Add up the digits of each point's id number and put the total in an attribute dsum.
Define a helper function window(x, lo, hi, w) = smooth(lo - w, lo, x) * (1 - smooth(hi, hi + w, x)) and use it twice: f@in_y = window(P.y, 0.2, 0.6, 0.1) and f@in_x = window(P.x, -1, 1, 0.5).
float window(float x; float lo; float hi; float w) { return smooth(lo - w, lo, x) * (1 - smooth(hi, hi + w, x)); }  f@in_y = window(P.y, 0.2, 0.6, 0.1); f@in_x = window(P.x, -1, 1, 0.5).

I need the same soft-edged window twice, so write it as a function: 1 between lo and hi, fading to 0 over a width w outside each end with smooth(). Apply it to the height (in_y: lo 0.2, hi 0.6, w 0.1) and to x (in_x: lo -1, hi 1, w 0.5).

Store in v@dir a direction inside a cone around the normalised point normal N with half-angle spread degrees (float parameter): sample_direction_cone(N, radians(spread), u) with the two random numbers u = (rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100)).
v@dir = sample_direction_cone(normalize(N), radians(chf("spread")), set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100))).
Scatter a launch direction dir around each normal, at most spread degrees (a parameter) away from it, using sample_direction_cone with the random pair (rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100)).
code:
vector2 u = set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100));
v@dir = sample_direction_cone(normalize(v@N), radians(chf("spread")), u);

prompts: Pick one index of the float array attribute samples at random, with probability proportional to the values in the array: i@pick = sample_discrete(samples, u) with the random number u = rand(@ptnum + 7).
i@pick = sample_discrete(f[]@samples, rand(@ptnum + 7)).
Treat each point's samples list as weights and draw one index from it (heavier entries more likely) into an attribute pick, using sample_discrete with rand(@ptnum + 7) as the random number.
code: i@pick = sample_discrete(f[]@samples, rand(@ptnum + 7));

prompts: Move every point onto a disk of radius radius (float parameter) in the XZ plane centred at the origin, uniformly distributed: with the 2D sample d = sample_circle_uniform((rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100))), set P = (d.x, 0, d.y) * radius.
vector2 d = sample_circle_uniform(set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100))); P = set(d.x, 0, d.y) * chf("radius").

Rearrange the points into an evenly filled flat disc on the ground (radius from a parameter radius), using sample_circle_uniform with the random pair (rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100)) for the x and z coordinates.
code:
vector2 d = sample_circle_uniform(set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum + 100)));
@P = set(d.x, 0, d.y) * chf("radius");

prompts: Add to P.y a normally distributed random offset with mean 0 and standard deviation sd (float parameter): sample_normal(0, sd, u) with u = rand(@ptnum + 11).
P.y += sample_normal(0, ch("sd"), rand(@ptnum + 11)).

Jitter the heights with a bell-curve distribution, most points near their original height and a few further away, with the standard deviation on a slider sd (use sample_normal with mean 0 and rand(@ptnum + 11)).
code: @P.y += sample_normal(0, ch("sd"), rand(@ptnum + 11));

prompts: Give all points that share the same name attribute the same random colour: Cd = the vector rand() of the integer string hash random_shash(name).
v@Cd = rand(random_shash(s@name)).
Colour the points by name so every name gets its own random but stable colour (Cd = vector rand of random_shash of the name).
code: v@Cd = rand(random_shash(s@name));

prompts: Make every polygon own its points: for each vertex create a copy of its point (with all point attributes), rewire the vertex to the copy, and remove the original shared points.
For every vertex v of every primitive: np = addpoint(0, vertexpoint(0, v)); setvertexpoint(0, -1, v, np); removepoint(0, old point).
Split the mesh so that no two faces share a point any more (like unique points in a Facet SOP): each corner gets its own copy of the point and the old points disappear.

From a primitive wrangle add one new point at the centre of every primitive (the primitive's P) and store the primitive's area (intrinsic measuredarea) in the float attribute area on that new point; existing points keep area 0.
pt = addpoint(geoself(), P); setpointattrib(geoself(), "area", pt, primintrinsic(0, "measuredarea", primnum)).
Drop a point into the middle of each face and tag it with that face's surface area in an attribute area (the original points are left alone and stay at 0).
Store in the vector array attribute npos the positions of the point's neighbours, in the order returned by neighbours().
foreach (n in neighbours(0, ptnum)) append(npos, P of n); v[]@npos = npos.
Each point should carry a list npos with the positions of all the points it is connected to.

Using the @group_ binding (i@group_core and i@group_shell), put every point closer to the origin than the float parameter radius into the point group core and every other point into the point group shell.
i@group_core = length(P) < chf("radius"); i@group_shell = !i@group_core.

Split the points into two groups around the origin with a slider radius: core for the points inside that distance, shell for the rest. Write the memberships through the group_core and group_shell bindings.
code:
i@group_core = length(@P) < chf("radius");
i@group_shell = !i@group_core;

prompts: Store in f@left how much of each particle's mass remains after its age when the mass halves every halflife seconds (float parameter): mass * exp(-log(2) * age / halflife).
f@left = mass * exp(-log(2) * age / chf("halflife")).

The particles lose substance over time with a half-life I set on a slider halflife: after that many seconds of age only half of the mass is left, after twice that a quarter. Write the remaining amount to left.
code: f@left = f@mass * exp(-log(2) * f@age / chf("halflife"));

prompts: If the geometry has a vector detail attribute tint, multiply the point colour Cd by it component by component; if there is no such detail attribute leave Cd unchanged.
if (hasdetailattrib(0, "tint")) { vector t = detail(0, "tint"); Cd *= t; }
Some of my inputs carry an overall tint colour as a detail attribute called tint. When it is there, tint all point colours with it; when it is not, do nothing.
Read the four-component parameter tint with chp and set Cd to its first three components and Alpha to its fourth.
vector4 t = chp("tint"); v@Cd = set(t.x, t.y, t.z); f@Alpha = t.w.
There is an RGBA parameter called tint on the node: colour the points with its RGB and put its alpha into the Alpha attribute.

If the integer toggle parameter unit is on (non-zero), normalise the velocity attribute v; if it is off leave v unchanged. In both cases store the original speed (length of v before any change) in f@speed.
f@speed = length(v); if (chi("unit")) v = normalize(v).
Add a checkbox unit: when ticked, velocities become unit length; either way keep the old speed in an attribute speed.
Read the string parameter mode: when it is "floor" set P.y to floor(P.y), when it is "ceil" set P.y to ceil(P.y), and for any other text leave P unchanged.
string m = chs("mode"); if (m == "floor") P.y = floor(P.y); else if (m == "ceil") P.y = ceil(P.y).
A menu parameter mode chooses how to snap the heights to whole numbers: floor snaps down, ceil snaps up, anything else does nothing.

In a primitive wrangle, using the float point attribute weight, store on every primitive: f@wmax the largest weight among its points, i@wmax_pt the point number that has that largest weight (when several points tie, the one that comes first in the primitive's vertex order), and f@wavg the average weight of its points.
f@wmax = max over p in primpoints(0, primnum) of weight[p]; i@wmax_pt = the argmax point (first one in primpoints order on ties); f@wavg = sum(weight[p]) / number of points.

Promote the point attribute weight to the faces three ways: wmax is the highest weight on the face, wmax_pt is which point carries it (the earliest corner wins a tie), and wavg is the mean weight of the face corners.

In a point wrangle, using the float primitive attribute risk: store in f@risk_max the largest risk among all primitives that use the point, and set i@disagree to 1 when the largest and smallest risk among those primitives differ by more than the float parameter gap (strictly greater), otherwise 0.
f@risk_max = max(prim(0, "risk", p)) over p in pointprims(0, ptnum); i@disagree = (max - min) > chf("gap").

Points should inherit the worst risk of the faces touching them (risk_max). Also flag with disagree = 1 the points where the touching faces are really inconsistent, meaning the spread between their highest and lowest risk is bigger than the parameter gap.

In a detail wrangle summarise the string point attribute kind: s[]@kinds lists the distinct values sorted alphabetically (use nuniqueval and uniqueval), i[]@kind_counts holds the number of points having each of them in the same order, and s@top_kind is the value with the most points (the alphabetically first one if several tie).
kinds = sort(unique values of point kind); kind_counts[i] = count of points with kind == kinds[i]; top_kind = kinds[argmax(kind_counts)], first on ties.

Give me a little report on the kind attribute on the detail: the list of kinds that occur (in alphabetical order) as kinds, how many points carry each as kind_counts, and which kind is the most common as top_kind, taking the alphabetically earlier one when counts are equal.

In a detail wrangle inspect the point attribute whose name is in the string parameter attr: store its component count in i@asize (0 when it does not exist) and a class code in i@akind: 0 if the attribute does not exist, 1 if it is a single integer, 2 if it is a single float, 3 if it is a float with 3 components, 4 for any other existing attribute (pointattribsize and pointattribtype).
i@asize = pointattribsize(0, chs("attr")); i@akind = 0 (missing) | 1 (int, size 1) | 2 (float, size 1) | 3 (float, size 3) | 4 (anything else that exists).

Tell me what kind of point attribute the parameter attr names. asize is how many components it has (0 if there is no such attribute), and akind is 0 for missing, 1 for a plain integer, 2 for a plain float, 3 for a float vector with three components, and 4 for everything else.

In a vertex wrangle write v@uvn: the vertex attribute uv rescaled separately for each primitive so that the vertices of that primitive span 0 to 1 in u and in v, i.e. (uv - min) / (max - min) per component, where min and max are taken over the uv of all vertices of the same primitive. If the span of a component is 0, that component is 0. The z component of uvn is 0.
uvn.x = span.x > 0 ? (uv.x - lo.x)/span.x : 0, same for y, z = 0, with lo / hi the component-wise min / max of uv over primvertices of the primitive.

Stretch the uvs of every face to fill the 0-1 square on their own: store as uvn, per vertex, how far its u and v lie between the lowest and the highest u and v of the face (a face with no extent in a direction gets 0 there), and put 0 in the third component.

In a point wrangle grow the existing point group seed by one ring of neighbours: create the point group grown containing every seed point plus every point that shares an edge with a seed point (use neighbours), and the point group ring containing only the points that were added, i.e. in grown but not in seed.
grown = seed + neighbours(seed); ring = grown - seed (point groups), with neighbours = points sharing an edge.

I have a selection called seed. Expand it by one step along the mesh edges into a group called grown, and also give me the group ring that holds just the newly selected points around it, without the original seed points.

In a detail wrangle build the point group picked: take the points of the groups named in the string parameter include (a space-separated list of group names, their union; use expandpointgroup) and leave out every point that belongs to the point group named in the string parameter exclude.
picked = expandpointgroup(0, chs("include")) minus members of group chs("exclude"), as the point group picked.

Two string parameters: include lists point groups separated by spaces, exclude names one group. Make a new point group picked from everything in the included groups except what is also in the excluded group.

In a point wrangle, accumulate summary values of the float point attribute temperature into detail attributes with setdetailattrib: the integer n_total (number of points), the integer n_hot (number of points whose temperature is strictly greater than the float parameter limit) and the float temp_max (the largest temperature).
n_total = count of points, n_hot = count of points with temperature > chf("limit"), temp_max = max(temperature), all as detail attributes written with setdetailattrib modes add / add / max.
I want the whole geometry summarised on the detail while running over points: how many points there are (n_total), how many are hotter than limit (n_hot), and the hottest temperature (temp_max).

In a point wrangle clean the integer array point attribute nbrs: write i[]@nbrs_clean with its values sorted ascending, each value kept once, and without the point's own number (@ptnum); also store in i@nbrs_removed how many entries of nbrs were dropped (duplicates and self entries together).
nbrs_clean = sort(unique(nbrs) minus {ptnum}); nbrs_removed = len(nbrs) - len(nbrs_clean).

The nbrs list on each point is messy: it repeats some points and even contains the point itself. Make nbrs_clean from it: ascending, no repeats, no self entry. And tell me in nbrs_removed how many entries had to go.

In a point wrangle promote the integer primitive attribute zone to the points by majority vote: i@zone_vote is the zone value that occurs most often among the primitives that use the point; when several values have the same highest count, the smallest value wins.
zone_vote = argmax over values v of count(prims of the point with zone == v), smallest v on ties; prims = pointprims(0, ptnum).
Every point should take the zone that most of its surrounding faces have, stored as zone_vote. If two zones are equally common, pick the lower number.

In a vertex wrangle find the next vertex of the same primitive (the following vertex in the primitive's vertex order, wrapping from the last back to the first) and store in f@uv_edge the distance between this vertex's uv and the uv of that next vertex, and in i@next_pt the point number of the next vertex.
next = primvertices(0, primnum)[(vertexprimindex(0, vtxnum) + 1) % count]; uv_edge = distance(uv, vertex(0, "uv", next)); next_pt = vertexpoint(0, next).

For every polygon corner, how long is the uv edge that leaves it towards the next corner of the face (the last corner connects to the first)? Store that length as uv_edge, and the point number of the corner it leads to as next_pt.

In a vertex wrangle write v@st: if the geometry has a vertex attribute uv (hasvertexattrib), copy this vertex's uv into st; otherwise use a planar projection set(P.x, P.z, 0) multiplied by the float parameter scale.
st = hasvertexattrib(0, "uv") ? uv : set(P.x, P.z, 0) * chf("scale").

I need texture coordinates called st on every corner. Use the geometry's own uv when it has them, and if it does not, project from above using x and z of the position (third component 0) times the parameter scale.

In a point wrangle remap the string point attribute kind with a lookup table: rock becomes stone, sand becomes dust, moss becomes grass; store the result in s@material (any other kind, such as ice, is copied unchanged). Also store in i@kind_id the position of kind in the list rock, sand, moss (0, 1, 2), or -1 when the kind is not in the list.
material = {rock: stone, sand: dust, moss: grass}[kind] else kind itself; kind_id = index of kind in (rock, sand, moss), -1 if absent.

Rename my kinds with a small table: rock to stone, sand to dust, moss to grass, saving the new name as material and leaving unknown names (ice) as they are. And save a number kind_id that is 0 for rock, 1 for sand, 2 for moss and -1 for anything else.

In a point wrangle promote the vertex attribute uv to the points: v@uv_avg is the average of the uv of all vertices that use the point, and f@uv_spread is the largest distance between uv_avg and any of those vertex uvs (0 where all vertices agree).
uv_avg = sum(uv of pointvertices(0, ptnum)) / count; uv_spread = max over those vertices of distance(uv, uv_avg).

Points sit on several corners and each corner may have its own uv. Give every point the mean uv of its corners as uv_avg, and measure how torn the point is with uv_spread, the biggest distance from that mean to one of its corner uvs.

In a detail wrangle count the primitives per value of the string primitive attribute name: store a dictionary d@piece_counts mapping each name to its number of primitives, the integer i@n_names with the number of distinct names, and s@largest with the name that has the most primitives (the alphabetically first one when counts tie).
piece_counts[name] = number of primitives with that name; n_names = len(piece_counts); largest = argmax over sorted(keys), first on ties.

How many faces does each named piece have? Put it into a dictionary called piece_counts on the detail, add n_names for how many different names exist, and largest for the name with the most faces (alphabetically first if there is a tie).

In a detail wrangle add a flat rectangular grid of points and quads in the XZ plane (y = 0), centred on the origin: the integer parameters nx and nz give the number of points along X and along Z (both at least 2) and the float parameter cell the spacing between neighbouring points. Point (i, j), i = 0..nx-1 along X and j = 0..nz-1 along Z, sits at ((i - (nx-1)/2) * cell, 0, (j - (nz-1)/2) * cell). Create the points row by row (j outer, i inner), then one quad for every grid cell, wound so that its normal points toward +Y.

P(i, j) = ((i - (nx-1)/2) * cell, 0, (j - (nz-1)/2) * cell) for i < nx, j < nz; quad(i, j) = points (i, j), (i, j+1), (i+1, j+1), (i+1, j) for i < nx-1, j < nz-1 (normal +Y). Parameters nx, nz (int), cell (float).

Build me a flat grid mesh lying on the ground (y = 0) and centred on the origin, made of quads. nx and nz are how many points it has in the X and Z directions, cell is the distance between neighbouring points. Quads must face up (normal toward +Y). Add it as new points and polygons; leave whatever geometry is already there alone.

In a detail wrangle create ONE open polyline through all points with a greedy nearest-neighbour walk: start at point 0, then repeatedly go to the nearest point (by distance between P positions) that has not been visited yet, until every point is visited once. If two candidates are equally near take the lower point number. The polyline's vertices are in visiting order and use the existing points (no new points).
path = [0]; while unvisited points remain: next = argmin over unvisited q of distance(P[last], P[q]) (lowest q wins ties); one polyline with vertices path[0], path[1], ... using the existing points.

Draw a single scribble line that touches every point once: begin at point number 0, always hop to the closest point you have not been to yet (if two are equally close, the lower number), and stop when all are visited. One open curve made from the existing points, vertices in the order visited.

In a primitive wrangle shorten every primitive to its first keep vertices (keep is an integer parameter, at least 1): remove the vertices with index keep, keep+1, ... from the primitive using removevertex. The points themselves stay in the geometry. Primitives that have keep vertices or fewer are not changed.
for i in keep .. vertexcount(prim)-1: removevertex(vertexindex(prim, i)); the points are not deleted.
Cut every curve short so that only its first keep points are still part of it (keep is an integer parameter). The cut-off points should stay in the geometry, they just no longer belong to the curve.

In a primitive wrangle replace every polygon by wireframe lines: add one two-point polyline for every UNIQUE edge of the polygon mesh (an edge shared by two polygons must give just one line, not two; use hedge_primary to pick one half-edge per edge), then delete the polygons themselves but keep all points. The direction of the lines does not matter.
for each half-edge h of the polygon: if hedge_primary(h) == h then addprim("polyline", hedge_srcpoint(h), hedge_dstpoint(h)); then removeprim(@primnum, 0).
Turn the mesh into a wireframe: one straight line per edge of the mesh, exactly one even where two faces meet at that edge, and no faces left over. The points stay where they are.

In a primitive wrangle split every quad (primitive with exactly 4 vertices, corners p0 p1 p2 p3 in vertex order) into two triangles along its SHORTER diagonal: if distance(p0, p2) <= distance(p1, p3) the triangles are (p0, p1, p2) and (p0, p2, p3), otherwise (p0, p1, p3) and (p1, p2, p3), with the points in the order listed. Delete the quad itself but keep all points. Primitives with other vertex counts are left unchanged.
quad = (p0, p1, p2, p3); d02 = distance(p0, p2), d13 = distance(p1, p3); d02 <= d13 ? tris (p0,p1,p2),(p0,p2,p3) : tris (p0,p1,p3),(p1,p2,p3); remove the quad; non-quads untouched.

Triangulate the four-sided faces, always cutting along whichever diagonal is shorter (p0-p2 wins a tie), so the triangles are less stretched. Corner order p0..p3 is the polygon's vertex order and each triangle lists its corners in the order of the original quad. Keep the points, leave triangles and bigger polygons alone.

In a detail wrangle trace the outer border of an open polygon mesh that has a single border loop and add it as one closed polygon (using the existing points, the mesh itself stays). A border half-edge is one with no equivalent half-edge on another polygon (hedge_nextequiv returns itself). Start with the first border half-edge found when scanning the primitives in order and, within a primitive, the vertices in vertex order; add the source point of the half-edge to the loop, then move to the border half-edge that starts at its destination point (pointhedge / pointhedgenext at that point) and repeat until you are back at the start half-edge.

h0 = first border half-edge (primitives ascending, vertices ascending); h = h0; do { push(loop, hedge_srcpoint(h)); h = the border half-edge among pointhedge(hedge_dstpoint(h)) .. pointhedgenext } while h != h0; addprim("poly", loop).

Make an outline polygon around the boundary of the open mesh: walk along the border edges in the direction the faces wind, starting from the first border edge you meet (go through faces in order, corners in order), until you return to the beginning, and create a single closed polygon from those points. The mesh stays.

For every point add up the corner angles of all polygon corners that use it: for each vertex of the point take the previous and next point of its polygon (wrapping around), the angle in degrees between the directions from the point to those two neighbours (acos of the dot product of the normalized directions), and sum them over all vertices of the point. Store the sum in f@anglesum and 360 minus the sum in f@defect. Walk the vertices of the point with pointvertex and vertexnext. A point with no vertices gets anglesum 0.
anglesum = sum over vertices v of P: degrees(acos(dot(normalize(prev - P), normalize(next - P)))), prev / next being the neighbouring points in v's polygon; defect = 360 - anglesum.

Measure how 'flat' the mesh is at each point: add up the angles (in degrees) of all face corners that meet at the point into anglesum (a flat interior point gives 360) and store the angle defect 360 - anglesum in defect. The angle of a corner is the angle between the two edges leaving the point toward the previous and next corner of that face.

In a detail wrangle unshare all points of the polygon mesh so that no two vertices use the same point: for every vertex of every primitive (primitives in order, vertices in vertex order) create a new point that is a copy of the vertex's current point (addpoint with the point number copies all its attributes) and rewire the vertex to it with setvertexpoint. Finally delete all the ORIGINAL points. Every primitive keeps its shape and vertex order.
for each vertex (prim, i): new = addpoint(0, vertexpoint(prim, i)); setvertexpoint(0, prim, i, new); then removepoint(0, p) for every original point p; result: #points = #vertices.

Split the mesh into loose faces: give every corner of every face its own private point at the same position (copying the old point's attributes), re-attach the corner to it, and throw away the old shared points. Faces must look identical afterwards but no longer share any point.

In a detail wrangle add copies of the whole polygon geometry: for c = 1 .. copies (integer parameter) create a duplicate of every point (only its position, shifted by c times the vector parameter offset) and of every polygon (same vertex order, using the duplicated points). The original geometry stays as it is, and copies do not share points with each other or with the original.
for c in 1..copies: new point for each original point p at P(p) + c * offset; new polygon for each original polygon with the same corner order on the new points; originals untouched.
