size = bmax - bmin; for each axis with P < bmin or P > bmax: P = bmin + (P - bmin) - floor((P - bmin) / size) * size. recycled = 1 if any axis was changed else 0; where recycled, age = 0. bmin and bmax are vector parameters; writes P, i@recycled and f@age.

Make an endless box of particles: whatever flies out through a wall of the box spanned by the vector parameters bmin and bmax re-enters through the opposite wall (the position is shifted by the box size along that axis, as many times as needed). A particle that had to be wrapped counts as newly recycled: flag it with an integer attribute recycled = 1 (others 0) and set its age attribute back to 0.

Initialise newly born particles: a particle is new if its float attribute age is smaller than the float parameter dt. Set i@born to 1 for new particles and 0 for the others. For new particles only: with the two uniform numbers u = set(rand(@id), rand(@id + 101)) (@id is the integer id attribute) set v = speed * sample_hemisphere({0, 1, 0}, u), and set the float attribute life = fit01(rand(@id + 7), lmin, lmax). speed, lmin and lmax are float parameters. Old particles keep v and life.

born = age < dt; if born: v = speed * sample_hemisphere({0, 1, 0}, set(rand(id), rand(id + 101))); life = fit01(rand(id + 7), lmin, lmax). dt, speed, lmin, lmax are float parameters; id is the integer point attribute id. Output i@born, v and life.

Birth setup for a particle system: everything younger than dt seconds (float parameter, age < dt) is flagged born = 1 (the rest 0) and receives a launch velocity of length speed in a random direction on the upper hemisphere around +Y, taken as sample_hemisphere({0, 1, 0}, u) with u = set(rand(@id), rand(@id + 101)), plus a random lifetime life = fit01(rand(@id + 7), lmin, lmax) with lmin and lmax float parameters. Older particles are left alone.

One Jacobi relaxation pass of distance constraints, run over primitives. Every primitive is a two-point constraint with the float primitive attribute restlength; the points have an integer attribute pin (1 = pinned) and a vector attribute dpos that starts at zero. With d = P1 - P0 and len = |d|, the correction c = relax * (len - restlength) * d / len (relax is a float parameter). Weights w0 and w1 are 1 for free points and 0 for pinned ones. If w0 + w1 > 0, add c * w0 / (w0 + w1) to dpos of point 0 and subtract c * w1 / (w0 + w1) from dpos of point 1, using setpointattrib on geoself() in "add" mode. Positions are not changed.

For each prim with points a, b: d = Pb - Pa, len = |d|, c = relax * (len - restlength) * d / len, wa = 1 - pin[a], wb = 1 - pin[b]; if wa + wb > 0: dpos[a] += c * wa / (wa + wb), dpos[b] -= c * wb / (wa + wb) (setpointattrib "add" on geoself()). relax is a float parameter; dpos (vector, starts at 0) accumulates over all prims touching a point.

Collect the position corrections that a soft-body/cloth solver would apply for one relaxation iteration without moving anything yet. Each two-point constraint primitive wants its points to be restlength apart (primitive attribute); it computes the stretch vector, takes the fraction relax (float parameter) of the length error, and hands it to its end points: the first point is moved toward the second and the second toward the first, shared between them, but a point with pin = 1 never receives anything, so the other one takes the whole correction. Everything is summed into the vector point attribute dpos (already present, zero) with setpointattrib add on geoself().

Collide the particles with the signed distance field named surface on the second input. With d = volumesample(1, "surface", P) and n = normalize(volumegradient(1, "surface", P)): if d < radius (float parameter, strict), the particle is in contact; move it out along n by radius - d (P += n * (radius - d)) and, if dot(v, n) < 0, remove the normal velocity and reflect it with the float parameter restitution: v -= (1 + restitution) * dot(v, n) * n. Set the integer attribute hit to 1 for particles in contact and 0 otherwise.

d = sdf(P); n = normalize(grad sdf(P)); hit = d < radius; if hit: P += n * (radius - d); vn = dot(v, n); if vn < 0: v -= (1 + restitution) * vn * n. sdf is the volume surface on input 1 (volumesample and volumegradient by name), radius and restitution are float parameters. Writes P, v, i@hit.

Bounce particles off the collision shape that comes in as the SDF volume surface on the second input. Particles whose distance to the surface is less than radius (float parameter) are pushed back out along the surface normal (the normalised gradient of the field) to exactly radius away, and a particle that is moving into the surface loses its inward velocity and gets it back reflected scaled by restitution (float parameter). Mark the touching particles with an integer attribute hit = 1, the rest 0.

Diffuse bounce on the ground plane y = 0: for every particle with P.y < 0, put it on the plane (P.y = 0) and give it a new velocity v = length(v) * restitution * sample_hemisphere({0, 1, 0}, set(rand(@id), rand(@id + 101))) (a random direction in the upper hemisphere, @id is the integer id attribute, restitution is a float parameter). Set the integer attribute bounced to 1 for those particles and 0 for all others, which are not changed.

if P.y < 0: P.y = 0; v = |v| * restitution * sample_hemisphere({0, 1, 0}, u) with u = set(rand(id), rand(id + 101)); bounced = (P.y < 0 before the change). restitution is a float parameter. Writes P, v, i@bounced.

Particles that fall through the floor (y below 0) should land on it and scatter: snap them to y = 0 and send them off in a random direction on the upper hemisphere (sample_hemisphere around +Y with u = set(rand(@id), rand(@id + 101))), keeping only the fraction restitution (float parameter) of their old speed. Flag those particles with bounced = 1 (integer attribute); everything else gets 0 and stays as it is.

Accumulate attraction toward the points of the second input, each with its own strength pscale: for every point a of the second input closer to the particle than the float parameter radius (use nearpoints on input 1), add k * pscale_a * (1 - d / radius)^2 * normalize(Pa - P) to the force, where d = |Pa - P| and k is a float parameter. Store the sum in v@force and the number of attractors in range in i@nattr.
force = k * sum over attractors a in input 1 with |Pa - P| < radius of pscale_a * (1 - |Pa - P| / radius)^2 * normalize(Pa - P); nattr = their count. radius, k are floats. Writes v@force and i@nattr.

Several magnets sit on the second input; the bigger their pscale the stronger they pull. Give each particle a total pull force in v@force: every magnet within radius (float parameter) contributes k (float parameter) times its pscale, times a falloff of (1 - distance/radius) squared, in the direction from the particle to the magnet. Also store how many magnets reach the particle in an integer attribute nattr.

Boids with a limited view: a neighbour is SEEN by a particle if it is another point closer than the float parameter radius (nearpoints) and the angle between the particle's velocity v and the direction to the neighbour is at most the float parameter fov degrees (use dot(normalize(v), normalize(Pn - P)) >= cos(radians(fov))). Store the number of seen neighbours in i@seen and in v@avoid the negative sum of the unit directions to the seen neighbours (zero if none).

seen = #{n != self : |Pn - P| < radius and dot(v/|v|, (Pn - P)/|Pn - P|) >= cos(radians(fov))}; avoid = -sum of (Pn - P)/|Pn - P| over those n. radius and fov (degrees) are float parameters. Writes i@seen and v@avoid.

Every particle can only see what is in front of it: other particles within radius (float parameter) and inside a cone around its heading v with half-angle fov degrees (float parameter, inclusive). Count them as seen (integer attribute) and make a steering-away vector avoid that is minus the sum of the unit vectors pointing to each of the seen particles, so that it points away from the crowd ahead.

In a volume wrangle on a heightfield write a slope mask into the mask layer. For the current voxel (indices ix, iy, iz) read the height layer with volumeindex at the neighbouring voxels ix+1 / ix-1 and iy+1 / iy-1 (same iz); dx is height(ix+1) - height(ix-1), dy is height(iy+1) - height(iy-1), and the slope is 0.5 * sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy) (a height change per voxel step, not per world unit). mask = smoothstep from the float parameter lo to the float parameter hi of that slope: 0 at or below lo, 1 at or above hi.

vector i = {ix, iy, iz}; dx = volumeindex(height, i + {1,0,0}) - volumeindex(height, i - {1,0,0}); dy = volumeindex(height, i + {0,1,0}) - volumeindex(height, i - {0,1,0}); @mask = smooth(lo, hi, 0.5 * length({dx, dy})) with float parameters lo and hi.

Paint the steep parts of the terrain into the mask layer: measure how much the height changes between the voxels on either side (central differences along both voxel axes, halved, combined as a vector length, per voxel step), and fade the mask smoothly from 0 at the float parameter lo up to 1 at the float parameter hi.

Sample the volume named density on the second input at each point (volumesample) into the float attribute dens. Set Cd to (clamp(dens, 0, 1), 0, 1 - clamp(dens, 0, 1)). Remove every point whose dens is less than or equal to the float parameter cut.
float d = volumesample(1, "density", P); f@dens = d; v@Cd = {c, 0, 1-c} with c = clamp(d, 0, 1); removepoint(0, ptnum) if d <= cut (float parameter).

Colour the points by the smoke they sit in: store the density of the second input's density volume at each point as dens, make the colour redder (red = dens clamped to 0..1) and less blue (blue = 1 minus that), and delete the points where the density is at most the parameter cut.

In a volume wrangle shift the density by a whole number of voxels along +X: the new density in the voxel with indices (ix, iy, iz) is the old density read with volumeindex(0, "density", {ix - shift, iy, iz}), where shift is an integer parameter. Do not change anything else.
@density = volumeindex(0, "density", set(ix - shift, iy, iz)), shift an integer parameter.

Slide the whole density field along the X axis by shift voxels (an integer parameter): what used to be in voxel ix should now appear in voxel ix + shift. Read the old values by voxel index; only the density changes.
code: @density = volumeindex(0, "density", set(@ix - chi("shift"), @iy, @iz));

prompts: In a detail wrangle look at the voxel with integer indices (a, b, c) (three integer parameters) of the volume named density. Store its world position from volumeindextopos in the vector detail attribute voxpos, its value from volumeindex in the float detail attribute voxval, and the distance of voxpos from the origin in the float detail attribute voxdist.
idx = {a, b, c}; v@voxpos = volumeindextopos(0, "density", idx); f@voxval = volumeindex(0, "density", idx); f@voxdist = length(voxpos).

Where in space is voxel (a, b, c) of the density volume, how much density does it hold, and how far from the world origin is it? Answer on the detail as voxpos, voxval and voxdist; a, b and c are integer parameters.

In a detail wrangle loop over all primitives of the input (all of them are volumes). Store in the integer detail attribute nvoxels the total number of voxels (the sum over the volumes of the product of the three components of volumeres), in the vector detail attribute maxres the component-wise maximum of volumeres over the volumes, and in the float detail attribute mindiam the smallest volumevoxeldiameter of any volume.
for pr in 0..nprimitives-1: r = volumeres(0, pr); i@nvoxels += int(r.x * r.y * r.z); v@maxres = max(maxres, r); f@mindiam = min(mindiam, volumevoxeldiameter(0, pr)).

Summarise the volumes on the input as detail attributes: nvoxels (int) is how many voxels they have all together, maxres (vector) is the largest resolution seen along each axis, and mindiam (float) is the smallest voxel diameter, as reported by volumevoxeldiameter.

In a volume wrangle on a heightfield dig a crater: let d be the distance in the XZ plane between (P.x, P.z) and (center.x, center.z), center being a vector parameter, and w = 1 - smooth(0, radius, d) with radius a float parameter. Subtract depth * w from the height layer (depth is a float parameter) and set the mask layer to max(mask, w).
w = 1 - smooth(0, radius, distance_xz(P, center)); @height -= depth * w; @mask = max(@mask, w).

Make a smooth round dent in the terrain around the point (center.x, center.z) with the vector parameter center: full depth (float parameter depth) at the centre, easing to no change at distance radius (float parameter), measured on the ground plane only. Also mark the dent in the mask layer, keeping any larger mask value already there.

In a primitive wrangle read the primitive intrinsic bounds (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) and store the extent of the primitive's bounding box in v@ext (max - min per axis). Also store in f@fill the primitive's measuredarea divided by the product of the two largest components of ext (0 if that product is 0).
float b[] = primintrinsic(0, "bounds", primnum); ext = {b[1]-b[0], b[3]-b[2], b[5]-b[4]}; sort the components; fill = measuredarea / (second largest * largest), 0 when that product is 0.

For each primitive give me the size of its bounding box as ext, and a fill ratio fill: how much of the biggest face of that box the primitive's area covers (area from the measuredarea intrinsic divided by the product of the two largest box dimensions, 0 for degenerate boxes).

In a detail wrangle work out the bounding box of every piece, a piece being all primitives that share the same string primitive attribute name. Take the distinct names in alphabetical order (uniquevals) and store them in the string array detail attribute names; in the vector array detail attributes bbmin and bbmax store, at the same index, the component-wise minimum and maximum of P over all points of the primitives with that name.
names = uniquevals(0, "primitive", "name") (sorted); for each name: bbmin[i] = min of point P over primpoints of the prims named so, bbmax[i] = the max; arrays s[]@names, v[]@bbmin, v[]@bbmax.

Give me one bounding box per piece (pieces are the groups of faces with the same primitive attribute name, listed in alphabetical order of name): detail arrays names, bbmin (lowest corner) and bbmax (highest corner), all with the same ordering. Use only the points of the faces carrying that name.

Each point has a string attribute path of the form /obj/geoN/part_MM (N and MM are numbers, MM may have a leading zero). Split it with split(path, "/") (which gives the three tokens obj, geoN, part_MM) and store the last token in the string attribute leaf, the integer N (digits of the second token, using re_replace("[^0-9]", "", token) and atoi) in the integer attribute geono, and the integer MM (the text of the last token after its final underscore, via re_replace("^.*_", "", leaf) and atoi) in the integer attribute part.
tk = split(path, "/"); s@leaf = tk[-1]; i@geono = atoi(re_replace("[^0-9]", "", tk[1])); i@part = atoi(re_replace("^.*_", "", leaf)).

Take the path attribute apart (it looks like /obj/geo3/part_07): leaf is the last path element as a string, geono is the number in the geo element as an int (3), part is the number after the underscore in the leaf as an int (7, no leading zeros).

Convert each point's Cd with rgbtohsv (hue 0..1, saturation, value). Store the hue in degrees (hue * 360) in the float attribute hue. Put the point in the point group warm when its saturation is greater than 0.4 and its hue in degrees is less than the float parameter hmax. Finally replace Cd by hsvtorgb of the same hue and value with saturation forced to 1.
vector hsv = rgbtohsv(Cd); f@hue = hsv.x * 360; group warm if hsv.y > 0.4 && hue < hmax (float parameter); Cd = hsvtorgb(set(hsv.x, 1, hsv.z)).

Find the warm, colourful points: work out each point's hue as an angle in degrees (attribute hue), and group (group name warm) those whose colour is clearly saturated (saturation above 0.4) and whose hue angle is under hmax degrees (float parameter). Afterwards make every colour fully saturated while keeping its hue and brightness.

Each point has a string attribute name made of letters followed by a number (like piece7). Let n = opdigits(name), the trailing number. Store n in the integer attribute num; store in the string attribute code the upper-cased letters part (name with its trailing digits removed by re_replace("[0-9]+$", "", name), then toupper), a minus sign and n zero-padded to 3 digits (sprintf %03d), e.g. PIECE-007; store in the string attribute letter chr(ord("A") + n % 26). Put the point in the point group even when name starts with the string parameter prefix (startswith) and n is even.

n = opdigits(name); i@num = n; s@code = sprintf("%s-%03d", toupper(re_replace("[0-9]+$", "", name)), n); s@letter = chr(ord("A") + n % 26); group even if startswith(name, prefix) && n % 2 == 0 (prefix a string parameter).

From names like piece7 derive three things: num, the number at the end (int), code, the upper-case word, a minus sign and the number padded with zeros to three digits (PIECE-007), and letter, the capital letter found by counting n steps from A and wrapping after 26 (n % 26). Also collect into the group even the points whose name begins with the string parameter prefix and whose number is even.
Split each point's velocity v into the component along its normal N and the component tangent to the surface; store them in v@vn and v@vt.
Decompose v into normal and tangential parts with respect to N (vn along N, vt perpendicular) and save both as vector attributes vn and vt.
I want to know how much of each point's motion goes into the surface versus slides along it: write the into-surface part of v to vn and the sliding part to vt.
Mirror every point across the plane through the origin whose normal is (1, 1, 0).
Reflect the geometry in the plane that passes through the world origin with normal direction (1,1,0).
Flip the model over a diagonal mirror standing at the origin, the mirror facing along (1,1,0).
code:
vector n = normalize({1, 1, 0});
@P -= 2 * dot(@P, n) * n;

prompts: Build an orthonormal frame from each point's normal N: tangentu = normalize(cross(up, N)) with up = (0,1,0), but use up = (1,0,0) when |N.y| > 0.99; tangentv = cross(N, tangentu) with N normalised.

Create two tangent vectors tangentu and tangentv perpendicular to N (and to each other). Reference axis: world Y, or world X when the normal is nearly vertical (|N.y| > 0.99). tangentu = normalize(cross(ref, N)), tangentv = cross(N, tangentu).
Make a stable surface frame per point from N (tangentu, tangentv), falling back to the X axis as reference where N points almost straight up or down (|N.y| > 0.99).
Rotate the geometry 90 degrees (positive by the right-hand rule) around the Z axis passing through the point (1, 0, 0).
Spin everything a quarter turn about a Z-parallel axis through (1,0,0), right-hand-rule positive.
Turn the model 90 degrees around a vertical-in-Z hinge located at x = 1 (right-hand rule).
Set p@orient so each point's local +Z axis points at the world origin, using the shortest-arc rotation from +Z.
Orient every point to face the origin: the rotation that takes (0,0,1) onto the unit direction from the point to the origin, stored as quaternion orient.
Make all the copies look at the centre: aim local Z at (0,0,0) with the minimal rotation, written to orient.
code: p@orient = dihedral({0, 0, 1}, normalize(-@P));

prompts: Each point has a 4x4 matrix xform. Store the point's position expressed in that matrix's local space in v@Plocal.
Transform P into the object space defined by the matrix attribute xform (apply the inverse) and save it as Plocal.
Where is each point relative to the frame xform? Write the local-space position to Plocal.
code: v@Plocal = @P * invert(4@xform);

prompts: Rotate each orient halfway back toward the identity rotation using spherical linear interpolation.
Blend the orientation quaternion 50% toward no rotation (identity) with slerp.
Relax every particle's rotation half the way to upright/unrotated, smoothly on the rotation sphere.
code: p@orient = slerp(p@orient, {0, 0, 0, 1}, 0.5);

prompts: Store in f@w a soft mask that is 0 in the bottom 20% of the bounding-box height, 1 in the top 20%, and eases smoothly (smoothstep) in between.
Create a height mask w using smooth() between normalised heights 0.2 and 0.8 (relbbox).
Fade a weight from 0 at the lower fifth of the object to 1 at the upper fifth with a soft S-curve.
code: f@w = smooth(0.2, 0.8, relbbox(0, @P).y);

prompts: Colour points by distance from the origin: blue at distance 0, red at distance 2 or more, linear in between.
Set Cd = lerp(blue, red, t) with t = distance to origin / 2, clamped to [0, 1].
Heat-map the points by how far they are from the centre, blue near, red at 2 units and beyond.
code:
float t = clamp(length(@P) / 2.0, 0, 1);
@Cd = lerp({0, 0, 1}, {1, 0, 0}, t);

prompts: Displace points in Y by three octaves of noise: frequencies 1, 2, 4 and amplitudes 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, each octave adding amplitude * (noise(P * frequency) - 0.5).
Fractal noise displacement on P.y: sum over 3 octaves of a*(noise(P*f)-0.5), starting f = 1, a = 0.5, doubling f and halving a each octave.
Make the surface bumpy with layered noise (3 layers, each twice as fine and half as strong, starting at frequency 1 strength 0.5), centred around zero, moving points up/down.
Move each point 30% of the way toward the point with the same number on the second input.
Blend positions: P = lerp(P, P of the matching point (same ptnum) on input 1, 0.3).
Morph the first input 30% toward the second one, point by point.
code:
vector q = point(1, "P", @ptnum);
@P = lerp(@P, q, 0.3);

prompts: Apply buoyancy for one step dt = 1/24: upward acceleration is 0.01 * (temperature - 295); update the velocity v.
Hot particles rise: add 0.01 * (temperature - 295) * dt to v.y with dt = 1/24 s.
Make warmer points float up: lift proportional to how much hotter than 295 they are (0.01 per degree), for one frame at 24 fps.
Each point belongs to a rigid body spinning with angular velocity w about its center attribute. Set v to the rigid-body velocity at the point.
Compute the velocity field of a rotating rigid body: v = w x (P - center) using the attributes w and center.
The pieces are spinning (w) around their centres; give each point its correct spin velocity.
code: v@v = cross(v@w, @P - v@center);

prompts: Give each particle the circular-orbit velocity around the world Y axis for GM = 4: speed sqrt(GM / r), r = distance from the axis, direction normalize(cross((0,1,0), radial)) where radial = (P.x, 0, P.z). Points on the axis keep their v.
Set v so every particle orbits the Y axis on a circle: centripetal balance GM/r^2 = v^2/r with GM = 4, tangent direction normalize(cross(up, radial)); leave particles on the axis alone.
Put the particles into stable circular orbits around the vertical axis (GM 4), moving along cross(up, outward direction).
Sum spring forces from edge neighbours into v@force: each edge is a spring with rest length 1 and stiffness 10, F = k (|d| - L) d/|d| with d from the point to its neighbour.
Accumulate Hooke's-law forces along all edges touching each point (k = 10, rest length 1) and store the total as force.
Compute the net pull each point feels from its connected edges acting as springs (stiffness 10, natural length 1).

Collide particles with a solid sphere of radius 1.2 at the origin: particles inside move to its surface along their radial direction, and if they are moving inward the inward radial part of v is removed.
Analytic sphere collider (r = 1.2, centre origin): project penetrating points onto the surface and cancel only the into-sphere normal velocity.
Keep particles out of a ball of radius 1.2: push intruders to the surface and stop them moving further in, letting them slide.
In a Volume Wrangle, multiply density by a factor that is 1 below y = -1, 0 above y = 1 and eases smoothly in between.
Volume wrangle: fade @density with height using 1 - smooth(-1, 1, y).
Fade the smoke out toward the top: full below -1, gone above 1, soft transition.
code: @density *= 1 - smooth(-1, 1, @P.y);

prompts: Volume wrangle: set density to 0 for voxels below the plane y = 0.
Clip the density field at the ground: zero everywhere y < 0.
Cut away all the fog under the floor (y below zero).
code: if (@P.y < 0) @density = 0;

prompts: Volume wrangle: replace density with the magnitude of the density gradient of the input volume.
Turn the density field into an edge-detection field: |volumegradient(0, 'density', P)|.
Show where the smoke density changes fastest: write the gradient length into density.
code: @density = length(volumegradient(0, "density", @P));

prompts: Put points whose normal is within 30 degrees of straight up into the point group flat.
Group as 'flat' every point with angle(N, +Y) < 30 degrees.
Select the gently sloped, upward-facing points (less than 30 degrees from vertical normal) into a group named flat.
code: if (dot(normalize(v@N), {0, 1, 0}) > cos(radians(30))) setpointgroup(0, "flat", @ptnum, 1);

prompts: Store each polygon's area (from the measuredarea intrinsic) in f@area and put polygons larger than the average polygon area into the primitive group big.
Use primintrinsic 'measuredarea': write it to area and group prims above the mean area as big.
Find the polygons that are bigger than average and group them as big; also keep each one's area.
Store the average point colour in the detail attribute avgCd and the point count in i@npts.
Detail wrangle: mean of Cd over all points -> v@avgCd, and npoints -> npts.
What is the overall average colour of the points? Put it on the detail as avgCd, plus how many points there are.
From the string attribute path (like /root/piece_3/mesh) store the second-to-last component in s@piece and its trailing number in i@pieceid.
Split path on '/' and keep the parent folder name (e.g. piece_3) as piece; parse the digits of it into pieceid.
Pull the piece name out of each path and its number as an integer.
Vertex wrangle: store in f@corner the interior angle in degrees of the polygon at each vertex.
For every vertex compute the angle between the edges to the previous and next vertex of its polygon (degrees) as corner.
Measure each polygon corner's angle and keep it on the vertex.
Delete every triangle (polygons with exactly 3 vertices), keep all other polygons.
Remove 3-sided primitives using primvertexcount.
Get rid of the triangles, keep quads and bigger.
code: if (primvertexcount(0, @primnum) == 3) removeprim(0, @primnum, 1);

prompts: Create a closed circle of 24 points with radius 2 in the XZ plane (point i at angle 2*pi*i/24, first on +X, then toward +Z) as one closed polygon.
Detail wrangle: build a 24-sided closed polygon circle, radius 2, lying flat (XZ), x = 2 cos(a), z = 2 sin(a).
Draw a flat ring outline: 24 evenly spaced points on a radius-2 circle around the origin, connected as one closed shape.
Create an open polyline helix of 60 points: radius 1, 3 full turns, rising from y = 0 to y = 3; point i at t = i/59, angle 2*pi*3*t, position (cos, 3t, sin).
Detail wrangle: spiral curve, 60 points, 3 turns, radius 1, height 3, starting at (1,0,0) turning toward +Z.
Make a spring shape: three loops of radius 1 climbing 3 units, 60 points, one polyline.
Fill the input's bounding box with a lattice of new points 0.25 apart starting at the box minimum: per axis floor(size / 0.25) + 1 points; loop x outermost, then y, then z. Keep the input geometry.
Add a grid of points (spacing 0.25, origin at getbbox_min) covering the bounding box, count per axis floor(size/0.25)+1, created in x-y-z nested order.
Scatter points on a regular 0.25 lattice through the object's bounding box (x outer loop, z inner).
Along the curve's vertex order, store the running sum of attribute w (including the current point) in f@wsum.
Prefix-sum w along the polyline and write the cumulative value to wsum.
Accumulate w from the start of the curve to each point (inclusive) into wsum.
Taper along Y: scale X and Z about the Y axis by 1 - 0.5 * h, where h is the point's normalised height in the bounding box.
Shrink the model toward the Y axis more the higher it is: factor 1 - 0.5 * relbbox(P).y on x and z.
Make it narrower toward the top: half width at the very top, full width at the bottom.
Push points away from (1, 0, 1) by 0.5 * (1 - smooth(0, 2, d)), where d is the distance to that point; a point exactly at the centre does not move.
